agent_notes: Psalm 10 has no superscription and continues Psalm 9 (the LXX and Vulgate join them; a partial acrostic runs across both). I translate it as the Hebrew stands, without harmonizing with Ps 9.

history.note: [consider] Gloss pos 5 as 'you hide' or 'you hide [your eyes]', in line with the commentary. (PS.10.1: 'תַּ֝עְלִ֗ים'; Rashi: 'תעלים עינים'.)

agent_notes: Ketiv/Qere in 10.10: Ketiv wĕdakkâ 'and crushed' vs Qere yidkeh 'he is crushed'; Ketiv ḥēlkāʾîm as one word vs Qere ḥēl kāʾîm 'a company of the wretched'. Subject of the crouching is the predator (Rashi, Metzudat David) as the lion image of 10.9 continues; Malbim's reading (old age) I do not follow. 'baʿăṣûmāyw' is uncertain ('by his mighty ones' vs 'by his bones/strength'). The reading is mine; the five English versions split over whether it is the poor or the predator who crouches (BBE has the upright crushed).

agent_notes: Qere ʿănāwîm 'humble' vs Ketiv ʿănîyîm 'poor' (Radak in the packet says ʿănîyîm is the older writing). I gloss the reading 'the humble' and mention the Ketiv in the commentary.

The five English versions split on תִּדְרֹשׁ (KJV 'thou wilt require it', YLT 'it is not required', BBE 'you will not make search for it'). I kept the plain verb 'seek' in the literal layer, with no object added, because the Hebrew has none; the dramatic layer supplies 'call to account' from the sense of דרשׁ in v.4 and v.15 (a judicial 'inquiry'). The speaker of 'you will not seek' is the wicked man, addressing God in his heart.

Corrected STEPBible 'mischief' for עָמָל to 'trouble' and 'vexation' for כַּעַס, and 'you pay attention' for תַּבִּיט to 'you look at'. Also corrected 'you are' for הָיִיתָ to 'you have been' (qatal). The word חֵלֶכָה is rare (also vv. 8, 10); I glossed it 'the wretched one' and treat the final ה as the form Radak calls an added he. The two-way reading of עָלֶיךָ יַעֲזֹב (the wretched 'leaves it to you' vs. 'abandons himself to you') is a real dispute; I followed the first, matching Metzudat David, Meiri and Radak.
The word רָאִתָה carries a written form missing its yod (Radak: 'ראתה חסרה היו״ד'); the packet shows it pointed fully. No effect on the translation.

history.note: [consider] Make the literal bracket '[it]' to match the gloss, the note and Radak's 'his case'. (PS.10.14: 'עָ֭לֶיךָ יַעֲזֹ֣ב חֵלֶ֑כָה'; Radak: 'עליך יעזב חלכה ... דינו'.)

agent_notes: Rashi's identification of the wicked as Amalek (and, in v.18, Esau) is not used in the translation. The final clause is a conditional-consequence ('you would seek ... you would not find'); both literal and dramatic layers keep the unmarked Hebrew and let the second-person imperfect carry it.

Revised after the reviewer's request: תַּקְשִׁיב is read as 2ms hiphil 'you cause [your ear] to attend' (the STEPBible morphology says 3fs). Ibn Ezra takes it as 3fs with 'your ear' as subject, the taw being the feminine marker. Both readings give the same sense, so the literal layer keeps 'you cause your ear to attend' and the commentary names the alternative without claiming any gender mismatch.

שמעת is a perfect, 'you have heard'. Radak takes it as 'you will hear' (like תשמע) and Meiri as a past form for the future; I keep the perfect as a statement of confidence, with the present sense in the dramatic layer. KJV 'thou wilt prepare' and 'thou wilt cause' turn the two imperfects into futures; the Hebrew imperfects are open between habitual and future.

history.note: [should_fix] Rewrite that sentence: תַּקְשִׁיב can be 2ms ('you cause your ear to attend') or 3fs with 'your ear' as subject ('your ear attends'); Ibn Ezra takes the second, reading the taw as the feminine marker. Drop the claim of a gender mismatch. (PS.10.17: 'תַּקְשִׁ֥יב אָזְנֶֽךָ' (morph HVhi3fs); Ibn Ezra: 'ותי"ו תקשיב אזנך סימן לשון נקבה'.)

agent_notes: Glosses corrected per the reviewer: pos 5 יוֹסִיף 'he will add / do again', pos 6 עוֹד 'again / any more'. The idiom יסף + infinitive means 'do again'.

לַעֲרֹץ is read as 'to terrify, strike with dread' (transitive, as Radak says), so the subject is the 'man from the earth' who terrifies. Ibn Ezra and Meiri allow the other reading, 'to be in dread of man'. The five English versions split: KJV and Webster 'oppress', ASV 'be terrible', BBE 'be feared', YLT 'oppress'. I chose 'terrify' as the root meaning. Rashi's identification of the one who adds no more with Esau is not carried into the text layers.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the commentary names both readings. (a) The greedy man is the subject of 'blesses' and 'spurns' (ASV, Rashi: the robber praises himself, 'I have spurned YHWH and I shall have peace'); (b) the wicked man blesses the greedy one (YLT, Radak, Meiri), and still spurns YHWH. The KJV makes YHWH the one who abhors, which turns the object of 'spurns' into its subject. The literal layer keeps the Hebrew's own ambiguity by putting 'one greedy for gain' first, as the Hebrew does. Ibn Ezra's reading of berekh as a noun ('gift') is quoted in the packet and I mention it only in the note on bērēkh.

STEPBible glosses hillel 'he boasts'; kept. I glossed nafsho 'his soul' (also throat or appetite) and left the sense to the commentary. In the dramatic layer I kept the ambiguity of who blesses whom rather than choosing.

agent_notes: The Hebrew is elliptic: 'wicked, like the height of his nose, does not seek; no God [is] all his schemes'. Five English versions split on whether 'bal yidrosh' has an object ('he will not require it' ASV/BBE) or 'seek God' (KJV). I supply [God] in brackets in the literal layer and mention the other reading. The accentuation (zaqef on 'raSha') also allows 'The wicked, in the haughtiness of his nose, does not seek'.

agent_notes: yāḥîlû: STEPBible glosses 'they endure'; I corrected to 'they prosper / are firm', following Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion (compare Job 20:21), against KJV/Webster 'grievous' (from ḥûl 'to writhe', Ibn Ezra's alternative). Qere darkāyw (plural) for Ketiv darkô (singular): 'ways' in both cases; I gloss the reading. Also yāpîaḥ: 'he puffs / snorts' (contempt), Radak gives also 'snare'.

Reviewer request addressed: Radak's references are now Josh 15:45, Isa 42:11 and Zech 2:8, cited as his. Lev 25:31 is dropped from sources and appears only as my own comparison in the commentary. The claim that the KJV softens 'murder' is removed; harag is a general verb for killing and 'murder' is defensible for 'the innocent'. The KJV point now made is about 'the poor' for the rare chelekhah.

chelekhah is rare and disputed: Rashi reads it as 'your host/army' (ḥēlekha, with the suffix -āh for -kha), Menachem as 'the wretched'; Radak and Metzudat Zion as 'poor, weak'. I glossed it 'the unfortunate [one]' after STEPBible and the English versions, and said in the commentary that the sense is uncertain. Verse 8 has plural 'eyes' with a plural verb yitzponu, as the Hebrew does.
